statement: In people who use cannabis, using it more often and starting younger are associated with a higher share meeting criteria for dependence in the figures that narrative reviews cite, but most of these figures are second-hand and rest on different designs and definitions, and in the one national survey analysis read that adjusted for other disorders, starting early went with a lower, not a higher, hazard of dependence. By frequency of use (second-hand): 17.0% of people who smoked cannabis weekly and 19.0% of those who smoked daily met dependence criteria, and 9.7% of people smoking weekly without dependence became dependent within a year (Cougle et al., 2016, as cited by Connor et al., 2021, which also calls this almost 1 in 19, although 9.7% is about 1 in 10); about 1 in 10 people who use regularly and up to one-third of people who use daily (a UN report cited by Connor et al., 2021); 30 to 40% of people with a history of daily use (two reviews cited by the same review); half of people who use daily, from a 3-year prospective study (van der Pol et al., 2013, as cited by Hall, 2015; its title refers to frequent use); and 25 to 50% of people who smoke daily, cited to a review that does not contain the figure (Volkow et al., 2014, citing Hall & Degenhardt, 2009), so it cannot be traced, and repeated without a citation in a 2020 professional statement (Page et al., 2020). No definitions or adjustment are given with these figures. By age of first use (second-hand): one in six of people who start in adolescence, against about 9 in 100 of everyone who has used (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009, and Hall, 2015, citing a 2006 book chapter for both figures; Volkow et al., 2014, citing Hall & Degenhardt for one in six, with 17% in its table, and the 2001-05 survey analysis for 9%); people who start in adolescence about 2 to 4 times as likely as people who start as adults to have dependence symptoms within 2 years of first use (Chen et al., 2009, as cited by Volkow et al., 2014); and first use before 16 linked to a higher risk and faster progression (Connor et al., 2021, citing three sources). In the 1990-92 US National Comorbidity Survey, by age at interview rather than age at first use, 15.3% (SE 2.3) of people aged 15 to 24 who had ever used cannabis had ever been dependent (DSM-III-R), against 8.1% at 25 to 34, 8.5% at 35 to 44 and 3.1% at 45 to 54, although the youngest had had the fewest years in which to become dependent; the authors cite studies in which people who start illicit drugs before 17 seem at higher risk of drug problems even after allowing for how long they had used, and note that differences between age groups may also reflect birth cohort, period and drug availability, and that deaths linked to dependence remove dependent people from older groups (Anthony et al., 1994). In the 2001-05 US NESARC (7,389 adults who had used cannabis; DSM-IV dependence; recalled ages), first use before 14, compared with first use at 14 or later, went with a higher hazard of dependence before adjustment (hazard ratio 2.47) and a lower one in the adjusted model (0.63, 95% CI 0.5 to 0.9), a model that stepwise selection built from sex, age, race or ethnicity, mood, anxiety and personality disorders, and dependence on nicotine, alcohol and cocaine (mood disorders, 2.69, and cocaine dependence, 4.14, among others, went with higher hazards); the authors suggest that the transition may come less from early onset itself than from the psychiatric and substance use disorders that go with it, and that people who start later may use more intensely and find cannabis easier to get (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). Because that model also adjusted for disorders that may have begun after first use, the reversal does not show that starting early protects against dependence (editors' reading). In a 3-year prospective study, measures of cannabis use itself did not predict who became dependent, while living alone, using cannabis to cope and negative life events did (van der Pol et al., 2013, as described by Curran et al., 2016, which calls its sample people who used daily; its title refers to frequent use), and twin studies find shared genetic and environmental influences on starting early (Connor et al., 2021). None of the sources measured how much THC people took, and, in the editors' reading, frequent use is partly built into what dependence means (its criteria include using more, or for longer, than intended and spending a great deal of time using), so the two are hard to separate. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Reviews report that people who use cannabis more often are more likely to be dependent: figures for people who use daily run from about 1 in 5 to 1 in 2, depending on the study, and one often-quoted figure (25 to 50 in 100) cannot be traced to any study. Reviews also say about 1 in 6 people who start as teenagers become dependent, against about 1 in 10 of everyone who has used. But in a large US survey, starting before age 14 went with more dependence only until other mental health and drug problems were taken into account; after that, it went with less. That does not mean starting early protects: some of those problems may have come after people started. So it is not clear whether starting young itself raises the risk or whether people who start young are at higher risk for other reasons. Most of these numbers are second-hand, and none of these studies can show cause. See the contested question.
population: People who use cannabis: US national survey samples (1990-92, ages 15 to 54; 2001-05, adults who had used) and the cohorts and surveys cited by narrative reviews for frequency and age of onset (definitions often not given)
exposure: Frequency of use (weekly, daily, regular, a history of daily use, frequent use, as each source defined it) and age at first use (adolescence, before 16, before 14); in one survey, age at interview
comparator: People who use less often or started later; in the 1990-92 survey, older age groups at interview
outcome: Cannabis dependence (DSM-III-R, DSM-IV, or as the cited studies defined it; dependence symptoms within 2 years of first use in one study)
magnitude: Second-hand frequency figures: 17.0% weekly and 19.0% daily meeting dependence criteria; 9.7% of weekly smokers without dependence dependent within a year (Cougle 2016 via Connor 2021); about 1 in 10 people who use regularly and up to one-third of people using daily (UN report via Connor 2021); 30-40% with a history of daily use (two reviews via Connor 2021); half of people using daily (van der Pol 2013 via Hall 2015); 25-50% of daily smokers (Volkow 2014, not traceable; repeated without a citation by Page 2020). Second-hand age figures: one in six with adolescent onset (book chapter via Hall 2009 and Hall 2015; 17% in Volkow 2014 Table 1); 2-4 times dependence symptoms within 2 years, adolescent against adult onset (Chen 2009 via Volkow 2014). NCS 1990-92 by age at interview, DSM-III-R dependence among people who had used: 15-24, 15.3% (SE 2.3); 25-34, 8.1% (0.7); 35-44, 8.5% (1.3); 45-54, 3.1% (1.5). NESARC 2001-05, first use before 14 (1,051 people, unweighted) against 14 or later (6,339): unadjusted HR 2.47 (95% CI 2.0 to 3.1); adjusted 0.63 (0.5 to 0.9); in the adjusted model male sex 1.44, age 18-29 3.09 and 30-44 2.46 (against 45 or older), mood disorder 2.69, anxiety disorder 2.31, personality disorder 2.30, nicotine dependence 2.06, alcohol dependence 2.55, cocaine dependence 4.14 (2.3 to 7.6).

risk_of_bias.note: Surveys and cohorts with self-reported, often recalled, use and ages; the age figures are unadjusted except in NESARC, where adjustment reversed the direction but conditioned on mood, anxiety and other substance use disorders entered as time-dependent covariates, some of which may follow early use; most frequency figures come with no adjustment set or definition (cards sc_anthony_1994, sc_lopez_quintero_2011, sc_connor_2021).

inconsistency.note: Figures for daily use run from 19% to about half across sources, and the early-onset association points in opposite directions before and after adjustment.

indirectness.note: Most figures are second-hand (narrative reviews; the studies behind them not read here, one a book chapter and one figure untraceable); the 1990-92 age groups are ages at interview, not at first use; DSM-III-R and DSM-IV dependence, not DSM-5 use disorder; frequency categories undefined.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded separately: most figures carry no interval, which is part of the second-hand problem; the one adjusted estimate (0.63, 0.5 to 0.9) excludes 1.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one level each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness: very low. Not upgraded for a dose-response gradient: the frequency gradient is second-hand, mostly cross-sectional and partly built into the outcome. Rated as worded, an association; whether frequent or early use causes dependence is the question in the debate box. Overlap: the one-in-six figure reaches three reviews from one source (a 2006 book chapter by the first author of the 1990-92 survey), Hall (2015) repeats Hall & Degenhardt (2009), and one 3-year study (van der Pol et al., 2013) is cited by two reviews for different findings (half of people using daily became dependent, Hall 2015; measures of use did not predict transition, Curran et al. 2016), so these are not independent replications. Status contested: for age of first use, crude figures and an adjusted national analysis point in opposite directions.

debate.question: Does using cannabis more often, or starting it younger, make dependence more likely, or do the people who use often or start young differ in other ways that explain the link?
debate.evidence_yes: Every source that reports dependence by frequency finds more in people who use more often: 17.0% of people who smoked weekly and 19.0% of those who smoked daily met dependence criteria, and 9.7% of people smoking weekly without dependence became dependent within a year (Cougle et al., 2016, as cited by Connor et al., 2021); a UN report gives about 1 in 10 people who use regularly and up to one-third of people who use daily, and two reviews 30 to 40% of people with a history of daily use (all as cited by Connor et al., 2021); and a 3-year prospective study is cited for half of people using daily (van der Pol et al., 2013, as cited by Hall, 2015), against about 9 in 100 of everyone who has used (see the claim on how many people become dependent). For age of starting, reviews give one in six of people who start in adolescence (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015; Volkow et al., 2014), describe people who start in adolescence as 2 to 4 times as likely as adult starters to show dependence symptoms within 2 years of first use (Chen et al., 2009, as cited by Volkow et al., 2014), and cite first use before 16 as raising the risk and speeding progression (Connor et al., 2021). In the 1990-92 US survey, 15.3% (SE 2.3) of 15- to 24-year-olds who had used cannabis had ever been dependent, against 8.1% to 8.5% at 25 to 44 and 3.1% at 45 to 54, although the youngest had had the fewest years at risk, and its authors cite studies in which people who start illicit drugs before 17 seem at higher risk of drug problems even after allowing for how long they had used (Anthony et al., 1994). Reviews also name concurrent tobacco use and male sex as risk factors (Curran et al., 2016).
debate.evidence_no: In the one national analysis read that modelled age of first use together with other risk factors (NESARC, 2001-05; 7,389 adults who had used cannabis; DSM-IV dependence), first use before 14 went with a higher hazard of dependence before adjustment (2.47) but a lower one in a model chosen by stepwise selection that kept sex, age, race or ethnicity, mood, anxiety and personality disorders and dependence on nicotine, alcohol and cocaine (0.63, 95% CI 0.5 to 0.9), while mood disorders (2.69) and cocaine dependence (4.14) went with higher hazards; the authors suggest that the transition may come less from early onset itself than from the disorders that go with it, and that later starters may use more intensely and find cannabis easier to get (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). A 3-year prospective study found that measures of cannabis use itself did not predict who became dependent, while living alone, using cannabis to cope and negative life events did (van der Pol et al., 2013, as described by Curran et al., 2016). Twin studies show genetic influence on starting early after allowing for other substance use, conduct disorder, depression and anxiety, and shared genetic or environmental factors contribute to early onset (Connor et al., 2021); a review names poor school achievement, deviant behaviour, rebelliousness, poor relationships with parents and parents' drug and alcohol problems as marking higher risk (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009). The widely quoted 25 to 50% of people who smoke daily is cited to a review that does not contain it (Volkow et al., 2014) and is repeated without a citation in a 2020 professional statement (Page et al., 2020), and the age-group figures from the 1990-92 survey are by age at interview, not age at first use, and may also reflect birth cohort, period, availability and deaths in older groups (Anthony et al., 1994).
debate.neither_can_show: Whether frequent or early use causes dependence: in every source people chose how often to use and when to start, most figures reach us through narrative reviews, and the sources behind one in six (a book chapter) and 25 to 50% (untraceable) cannot be checked here. Frequency and dependence are entangled: the dependence criteria include using more, or for longer, than intended and spending a great deal of time using (Curran et al., 2016, Box 3), so people may use more often because they are dependent. Ages of first use and of onset were recalled, sometimes decades later. Adjusting for other psychiatric and substance use disorders removes confounding where those disorders came first, but where they followed cannabis use it may also remove part of a real effect (editors' point; the NESARC models entered mood, anxiety and other substance use disorders as time-varying). None of the sources measured how much THC people took (Connor et al., 2021).
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). More frequent use goes with more dependence in every source that reports it, but the size depends on design and definition (from about 1 in 5 to about 1 in 2 of people using daily), most figures are second-hand, and one widely quoted figure cannot be traced. For age of starting, the crude figures point to more dependence in early starters, but the one national analysis that adjusted for other disorders found the opposite, which fits early starting being a marker of other risks at least as well as a cause; because that analysis also adjusted for disorders that may follow early use, it does not show that early starting protects, and the evidence read here does not settle which reading is right.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts that follow people from before first use, with repeated DSM-5 assessments and measured THC exposure (standard units and product strength), reporting the cumulative probability of use disorder by frequency, age of first use and product, with psychiatric problems dated before and after first use; and sibling or co-twin comparisons of early and late starters.
